lessons.title: Case Study: How Two Indian Companies Funded Growth in Opposite Ways

children.text: Two Indian retailers. Both scaled through the same consumer boom, both sold groceries and general merchandise to the same middle class, both were run by well-known founders. One of them is among the most valuable listed retailers in India. The other was ordered into liquidation in July 2024.
The difference was not the idea, the market or the execution alone. It was how each chose to pay for growth. This final lesson puts the whole course to work on one comparison.

body.text: Growth funded by cash compounds slowly and survives a shock. Growth funded by debt compounds quickly and requires that nothing goes badly wrong for as long as the debt lasts.

children.text: Company One: Avenue Supermarts, the Owner of DMart
Radhakishan Damani founded DMart in 2002 and grew it in a way that looked almost obstinately slow to competitors. Stores were added in small numbers each year, concentrated in
cluster expansion
around existing regions, and the company bought its store properties instead of leasing them.

markDefs.definition: Opening stores densely within a region before entering a new one, so distribution, supply and brand awareness are shared across nearby outlets.

children.text: Owning property
meant heavy upfront capital expenditure, but no rent escalation for the next twenty years and an asset that could be charged if borrowing was ever needed.
Everyday low pricing
meant thin margins, funded by very high stock turnover rather than by trade credit games.
Slow store addition
meant growth was limited to what operating cash and modest borrowing could fund.

body.title: Avenue Supermarts: funding a slow compounder

events.title: Private and largely self-funded
events.description: Growth paced to internally generated cash and limited debt. The company stayed unlisted for fourteen years, which meant no public pressure to accelerate.

events.title: IPO of ₹1,870 crore
events.description: Around ₹1,080 crore of the proceeds went to prepaying or repaying loans and redeeming non-convertible debentures, and about ₹366.6 crore to constructing and fitting out new stores. The listing was used mainly to clean up the balance sheet.

events.title: QIP at ₹2,049 per share
events.description: A qualified institutional placement raised roughly ₹4,000 crore from institutions, priced off the market, at a time of strength rather than need.

events.title: Low leverage maintained
events.description: Expansion continued to be funded largely from operations and equity rather than from rising borrowings.

body.title: What the IPO was really for
body.prompt: Of the ₹1,870 crore raised in the DMart IPO, about ₹1,080 crore went to repaying debt. What percentage of the issue was that? Answer to one decimal place.
body.explanation: ₹1,080 crore divided by ₹1,870 crore is about 57.8%. More than half the IPO was balance sheet repair, not expansion. The company used the public market the way Chapter 1 described reason four: fixing the funding structure, from a position of choice rather than distress.

body.text: Look at the sequence: repay debt at the IPO in 2017, then raise equity again through a QIP in 2020 when the shares were richly valued. That is the textbook use of listing, and the opposite of raising because the bank balance forced it. The company controlled the timing every time.

children.text: Company Two: Future Retail

Kishore Biyani built modern Indian retail. Big Bazaar, Food Bazaar and later Easyday brought organised retail to hundreds of Indian towns, and for years the group was the reference point for the whole sector. Its funding model was the mirror image of DMart's.
Leased stores
meant faster expansion with less capital upfront, and a fixed rental obligation in every location regardless of how each store performed.
Growth by acquisition
brought scale quickly, funded substantially by borrowing.
Working capital stretched across suppliers
, so a large base of
operational creditors
was effectively funding the business alongside the banks.

markDefs.definition: Suppliers and service providers owed money by a company, as distinct from financial creditors such as banks and bondholders.

body.title: Future Retail: what happened when the shock came

events.title: Debt-funded expansion
events.description: Rapid store growth and acquisitions built national scale, financed largely with borrowings against a business with thin margins and heavy fixed costs.

events.title: The shock and the default
events.description: Pandemic lockdowns closed stores while rent, salaries and interest continued. The company missed payments on its debt.

events.title: The rescue that did not close
events.description: Reliance Retail agreed to acquire the Future group retail assets in a transaction valued at ₹24,713 crore. Amazon challenged it in arbitration, and the deal never completed.

events.title: Into insolvency
events.description: Lenders moved to insolvency and the NCLT admitted Future Retail in July 2022, with dues of roughly ₹17,000 crore to financial and operational creditors.

events.title: One bid, rejected
events.description: Space Mantra emerged as the sole resolution applicant with a bid of about ₹550 crore. Lenders rejected it and the resolution professional moved for liquidation.

events.title: Liquidation ordered
events.description: The NCLT Mumbai bench ordered liquidation after the insolvency process exceeded its permissible period without an approved resolution plan.

body.title: The size of the loss
body.prompt: Space Mantra bid about ₹550 crore against dues of roughly ₹17,000 crore. What recovery would that have represented, as a percentage? Answer to one decimal place.
body.explanation: ₹550 crore divided by ₹17,000 crore is about 3.2%. Lenders rejected it, and liquidation followed. Set this against the ₹24,713 crore Reliance transaction that did not complete: the value of a retail business is its stores, staff and supplier relationships, and those decay fast once a company stops operating normally.

body.text: Time destroyed most of this value, exactly as Lesson 3.4 described. A business worth tens of thousands of crore to a strategic buyer in 2020 attracted a single bid of a few hundred crore by 2023. Leverage did not just create the crisis. It removed the company's ability to wait for a better outcome.

children.text: The Same Decade, Two Funding Philosophies

body.title: How each company answered the questions in this course

columns.label: Avenue Supermarts (DMart)
points: Growth paced to internally generated cash
Owned property: high capex, no rent escalation, chargeable assets
Low borrowings relative to net worth
IPO used substantially to repay debt
QIP raised from a position of strength, at a high price

columns.label: Future Retail
points: Growth paced to what lenders would fund
Leased property: low capex, permanent fixed rental obligations
Debt used to fund expansion and acquisitions
Rescue attempted only after default, with no leverage in the negotiation
Faster store additions, no cushion for a shock

body.caption: What each test from Lesson 5.1 would have said

cells: Certainty of returns
A new store in a proven cluster had predictable economics
Acquisitions and new formats carried far less certain returns
Bad-year servicing
Low fixed obligations, so a weak year was survivable
Rent plus interest continued through a year with almost no sales
Security available
Owned real estate could be charged if needed
Leased stores offered lenders little to take
Existing leverage
Deliberately kept low, with headroom preserved
High, leaving no capacity when the shock arrived
Speed versus certainty
Accepted slower growth for control of timing
Chose speed, and lost control of timing entirely

body.title: What was the decisive difference?
body.question: Both companies faced the same pandemic. What best explains why one continued operating and the other ended in liquidation?
options: DMart had low fixed obligations and headroom, so a collapse in sales was survivable, while Future Retail had rent and interest continuing against almost no revenue
Future Retail was in a worse location mix
The pandemic affected only leased stores
body.explanation: The shock was identical and external. What differed was the obligation structure each company had chosen years earlier. Owning property removed rent, low borrowing removed interest pressure, and headroom meant the company could absorb a bad year. Future Retail had committed to paying regardless of revenue, which is the defining feature of debt.

body.title: Was equity the answer for Future Retail?
body.question: Could Future Retail have avoided this outcome simply by raising equity instead of debt at every stage?
options: Not necessarily. Equity is more expensive and would have diluted the promoters heavily, but it would have removed the fixed obligations that turned a revenue shock into a default
No, because equity investors would not fund retail
Yes, because equity investors would have taken over management earlier
body.explanation: This is the honest answer. Equity would have cost the promoters a great deal of ownership, and would not have fixed thin margins or a leased cost base. What it would have done is remove the fixed payments, which is what converted a bad trading year into insolvency. The trade in this course is exactly that: ownership given up in exchange for the right to have a bad year.

children.text: It is worth being fair to a company that built an industry. Three things are true at once.
The shock was genuine and external.
No 2019 business plan modelled months of closed stores. Plenty of low-debt retailers also suffered badly.
The Amazon arbitration was outside the company's control
once it had begun, and it prevented an agreed rescue from completing.
And the leverage was a choice.
It was made years earlier, in good conditions, and it determined how much bad news the company could absorb before it lost the ability to decide its own future.

That is the useful way to read any corporate failure. The trigger is usually external and unpredictable. The capacity to survive it is internal and was decided in advance, on a day when everything looked fine.
Six Lessons to Take Into Your Own Decisions

body.title: The one-sentence summary of the course
body.textWithBlank: Debt is cheaper, keeps your ownership, and demands payment whatever happens. Equity is expensive, takes a permanent share of your company, and demands ___.
body.explanation: That single asymmetry explains every decision in this course. Debt costs less precisely because the lender is protected. Equity costs more precisely because the shareholder is not.

body.title: Your own company, one page
body.scenario: Take the organisation you actually work in, or one you know well. It may be a startup, a family business, a large listed corporate or the Indian arm of a multinational. Apply the whole course to it.
body.prompt: Write a one-page funding note covering: how the business is funded today, whether that mix suits the certainty of its cash flows, how much debt capacity it has left, and what you would recommend for its next significant requirement.
body.modelAnswer:
A good answer will work through the following, in roughly this order.

1. The current mix. Net worth against total borrowings, and the debt to equity ratio. For a listed company, pull this from screener.in as in Lesson 5.2. For a private one, take it from the latest audited balance sheet.

2. Whether the mix fits the business. Compare return on capital employed with the after-tax cost of debt. If ROCE is comfortably higher, leverage is working. If it is close or below, more debt is destroying value, whatever the accounts show.

3. The bad-year test. Find the worst EBITDA of the last five to seven years and recompute interest cover at that level. If cover falls below about 2x, the company is carrying more debt than its own volatility justifies.

4. Debt capacity and headroom. Sustainable EBITDA times a target multiple appropriate to the industry, less existing debt. Note that this number is set by the business, not by what a bank has offered.

5. Fixed obligations beyond borrowings. Leases, guarantees given to group companies, and contingent liabilities in the notes. Future Retail's rent was not in the Borrowings line and it was every bit as fixed as interest.

6. The next requirement. State what the money is for, how certain its returns are, and over what period it comes back. Then apply the eight tests from Lesson 5.1 and say which source follows, including the possibility of splitting it: debt for the contracted part, equity or internal accruals for the uncertain part.

7. What would make you wrong. Name the scenario in which your recommendation fails, and what the company would do then. A funding recommendation without that paragraph is not finished.

If you cannot get all the figures, write down which ones are missing and who in the organisation holds them. Knowing exactly which number you need is most of the work.

body.title: The course in one checklist
steps: Know why the money is being raised: growth, working capital, acquisition, balance sheet repair or survival
Match the instrument to the life stage of the company
Understand what selling equity permanently transfers: profits, votes, board seats and consent rights
For any borrowing, read the tenure, the security, the covenants and the personal guarantees, not just the rate
Convert costs to an after-tax basis before comparing debt with equity
Test leverage against your worst year, not your average one
Keep debt capacity in reserve so you can act when others cannot
Raise before you need to, so you keep the right to walk away

body.label: screener.in
body.description: Look up both Avenue Supermarts and any leveraged retailer, and compare ten years of Borrowings, Reserves and ROCE side by side. The two funding philosophies in this lesson are visible in the numbers long before they show up in the news.

cards.definition: ₹1,870 crore raised, with about ₹1,080 crore used to repay debt and redeem NCDs.
Roughly ₹4,000 crore raised from institutions at ₹2,049 per share, from a position of strength.
Owning stores means heavy capex but no rent escalation and chargeable security. Leasing means fast growth and permanent fixed obligations.
Reliance Retail transaction valued at ₹24,713 crore, challenged by Amazon and never completed.
Admitted to insolvency with dues of roughly ₹17,000 crore.
NCLT Mumbai ordered liquidation in July, after a sole bid of about ₹550 crore was rejected.
Unused debt capacity, which is what lets a company survive a shock and act during one.
Debt is cheaper and demands payment regardless. Equity is expensive and demands nothing in cash.

points: Two Indian retailers in the same decade chose opposite funding models, and the funding model decided which survived a common shock.
DMart grew slowly on internal cash and owned property, then used its IPO mainly to repay debt and a later QIP to raise from strength.
Future Retail grew quickly on borrowed money and leased stores, and had no cushion when revenue stopped.
Rent is as fixed as interest. Obligations outside the Borrowings line count just as much.
Once a company is in distress, time destroys value: ₹24,713 crore on the table in 2020, a rejected ₹550 crore bid by 2023.
The trigger for failure is usually external. The capacity to survive it is a funding decision made years earlier.
That is the whole course: debt is cheaper and unforgiving, equity is expensive and patient, and the right answer depends on how certain your cash flows really are.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not investment advice. It describes publicly reported events concerning real Indian companies, drawn from news reports and filings at the time, and is not a comment on the conduct of any individual or organisation. Several of these matters involved litigation and appeals. Nothing here is a recommendation to buy or sell any security.
